name: Operating Systems
description: Kernels, processes, scheduling, system calls, file systems and I/O — the layer everything else stands on.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Operating Systems is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is an operating system, and what does it do?
cards.answer: The software that manages the computer's hardware and gives programs a safe, uniform way to use it. It schedules programs onto the CPU, manages memory, provides files and devices, handles networking and enforces security between users and processes.
cards.explanation: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are operating systems. Without one, every program would have to drive the hardware itself — and any program could crash or spy on all the others.

cards.prompt: What is the kernel?
cards.answer: The core of the operating system that runs with full hardware privileges (kernel mode). It manages the CPU, memory and devices; ordinary programs run in a restricted user mode and must ask the kernel for anything privileged.
cards.explanation: The Linux kernel is just the kernel — a full "Linux" system adds tools, libraries and a desktop on top, typically from GNU and a distribution such as Ubuntu or Fedora.

cards.prompt: What is a process?
cards.answer: A running instance of a program: the code plus its own private memory, open files, and one or more threads. Opening the same program twice creates two separate processes.
cards.explanation: The OS isolates processes from each other, so one crashing does not take down the rest. Task Manager (Windows), Activity Monitor (macOS) and `ps`/`top` (Linux) list them.

cards.prompt: What is a system call?
cards.answer: The way a program asks the kernel to do something it cannot do itself — open a file, read from the network, start a process, allocate memory. Library functions such as `open()` or `print` end up making system calls.
cards.explanation: System calls are the boundary between user mode and kernel mode. Tools such as `strace` (Linux) let you watch every system call a program makes, which is a powerful debugging trick.

cards.prompt: What is a file system?
cards.answer: The part of the OS that organises data on storage into files and directories (folders), keeping track of names, sizes, permissions and where each file's bytes physically live.
cards.explanation: Common file systems: NTFS (Windows), APFS (macOS), ext4 and XFS (Linux), FAT32/exFAT (USB sticks). They differ in maximum file sizes, journaling (crash safety) and features such as snapshots.

cards.prompt: What is a device driver?
cards.answer: Software that lets the operating system talk to a specific piece of hardware — a graphics card, Wi-Fi chip or printer — translating generic OS requests into that device's commands.
cards.explanation: Drivers usually run inside the kernel, so a buggy driver can crash the whole system; many "blue screens" on Windows are driver faults.

modules.name: Kernel, Processes & Scheduling
modules.description: Privilege levels, process lifecycle, context switches and how the CPU is shared.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode, and how do you cross the boundary?
cards.answer: User mode restricts access to hardware and privileged instructions; kernel mode has full access. You cross deliberately with a system call (a trap instruction), or involuntarily via an interrupt or fault.
cards.explanation: The boundary is what makes isolation possible: a user process cannot touch another's memory or the disk directly, only ask the kernel to. Each crossing costs hundreds of cycles plus cache effects, which is why batching syscalls (io_uring, writev) matters in hot I/O paths.

cards.prompt: On Linux, you can see exactly which system calls a program makes by running `___ ./program`.
cards.answer: strace
cards.explanation: `strace` traces syscalls and signals, `ltrace` library calls, and `perf` gives sampled profiles. Reaching for strace when a process 'hangs' usually answers the question in seconds — it is almost always blocked in a read, a poll or a futex.

cards.prompt: What do `fork` and `exec` do, and why are they separate?
cards.answer: `fork` duplicates the current process (copy-on-write); `exec` replaces the process image with a new program. Separating them lets the child adjust its environment — redirect file descriptors, change user, set limits — between the two.
cards.explanation: That gap is how shells implement pipes and redirection. The cost is that fork copies page tables of a large parent; `posix_spawn` and `vfork` exist for the common spawn-and-exec case, and `fork` in a multithreaded process is a well-known footgun.

cards.prompt: What does a context switch cost?
cards.answer: Saving and restoring registers is a microsecond or so, but the real cost is indirect: cold caches and TLB entries for the incoming task. A process switch also changes the address space, flushing more state than a thread switch.
cards.explanation: This is why oversubscribing threads hurts throughput, why pinning threads to cores helps latency-sensitive systems, and why green threads or async I/O — which switch in user space without touching the kernel — scale so much better for I/O-bound concurrency.

cards.prompt: Zombie process vs orphan process
cards.answer: A zombie has exited but its exit status has not been reaped by its parent; an orphan is still running but its parent died.

left.title: Zombie
points: Holds only a PID and exit status
Caused by a parent that never calls wait()

cards.explanation: This matters in containers: PID 1 in a container is your app, and if it does not reap adopted children you accumulate zombies. That is why `--init` or a tiny init like tini exists.

modules.name: Memory, Files & I/O
modules.description: Paging, file descriptors, buffering and the I/O models.

cards.prompt: What is a page fault, and when is it expensive?
cards.answer: A page fault occurs when a process touches a virtual page with no valid mapping. Minor faults are resolved from memory (page cache, copy-on-write) and are cheap; major faults require disk I/O and cost milliseconds.
cards.explanation: Watch major faults, not total faults. Thrashing — where the working set exceeds RAM and every access faults — turns a healthy system into an unresponsive one, which is why the OOM killer often beats swapping to death.

cards.prompt: What is a file descriptor, and why is 'everything is a file' useful?
cards.answer: A small integer indexing the kernel's per-process table of open resources. Because files, sockets, pipes, devices and timers all appear as descriptors, the same `read`/`write`/`poll` calls work on all of them.
cards.explanation: That uniformity is why shell pipelines, `select`/`epoll` event loops and redirection compose so well. The limit (`ulimit -n`) is a classic production ceiling — 'too many open files' usually means leaked sockets, not too many files.

cards.prompt: Blocking I/O vs non-blocking with an event loop
cards.answer: Blocking parks the thread until data is ready; non-blocking returns immediately and you multiplex readiness with epoll/kqueue/IOCP.

left.title: Blocking
points: Memory and switching cost scales with connections
Fine up to a few thousand

right.title: Non-blocking + poller
points: One thread handles thousands of sockets
Any blocking call poisons the loop
More complex error and lifecycle handling

cards.explanation: `select` is O(n) per call and capped at FD_SETSIZE; `epoll` is O(1) with edge- or level-triggered notification. `io_uring` goes further with submission/completion rings that avoid syscalls per operation entirely.

cards.prompt: Your program's log output vanishes when it crashes, but appears when run in a terminal. Why?
cards.answer: stdout is line-buffered on a TTY and block-buffered when redirected to a file or pipe. On a crash the userspace buffer is never flushed. Flush explicitly, or switch to unbuffered/line-buffered mode.
cards.explanation: In Python, `python -u` or `flush=True`; in C, `setvbuf`; in containers, this is why logs appear in bursts. stderr is unbuffered by default — which is exactly why diagnostics belong there.
cards.code:
$ ./app > app.log      # crashes after printing a few dozen lines
$ wc -l app.log
0 app.log

$ ./app                # same binary, straight to the terminal
starting up...
processing batch 1

cards.prompt: Your container is killed during deploys and drops in-flight requests. Which signals are involved and what should the app do?
cards.answer: The orchestrator sends SIGTERM, waits a grace period, then SIGKILL (which cannot be caught). The app should catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, close resources and exit before the deadline.
cards.explanation: Two common traps: the signal goes to PID 1, so a shell-form entrypoint that does not `exec` swallows it; and the readiness probe must fail *before* shutdown starts so the load balancer stops sending traffic first.

modules.name: Scheduling, IPC & Storage
modules.description: CPU scheduling, priorities, inter-process communication, filesystems and inodes, the page cache and fsync.

cards.prompt: What does a CPU scheduler balance, and how does Linux's scheduler decide what runs?
cards.answer: Throughput, latency (responsiveness) and fairness. Linux long used CFS, which tracks each task's virtual runtime and runs the one that has had the least, weighted by its nice value; since 6.6 it uses EEVDF, which adds latency-aware deadlines. Real-time classes (`SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR`) preempt normal tasks.
cards.explanation: Preemptive schedulers interrupt a running task when its time slice ends or a higher-priority task wakes, so one busy loop cannot freeze the system. `nice`/`renice` adjust relative weights; CPU pinning (`taskset`) and cgroup CPU limits shape where and how much a process may run.

cards.prompt: What mechanisms can processes use to communicate?
cards.answer: Pipes (a byte stream between related processes) and named pipes (FIFOs); Unix domain sockets (bidirectional, local, can pass file descriptors); TCP/UDP sockets (local or remote); shared memory (fastest, but needs separate synchronisation); message queues; signals (tiny notifications); and files or memory-mapped files.
cards.explanation: Unix sockets are the workhorse for local services — Docker, Postgres and systemd all expose them — and are faster than loopback TCP. Shared memory avoids copying but brings every concurrency hazard of threads to processes.

cards.prompt: What is an inode, and what does a directory actually contain?
cards.answer: An inode stores a file's metadata — owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count — and pointers to its data blocks, but not its name. A directory is a table mapping names to inode numbers.
cards.explanation: That separation explains hard links (two names, one inode), why renaming within a filesystem is instant (only a directory entry changes), and why a filesystem can run out of inodes with free space remaining. `ls -i` shows inode numbers; `stat` shows the metadata.

cards.prompt: This "safe" config save can leave an empty or truncated file after a power cut. Why, and what is the correct pattern?
cards.code:
with open('config.json', 'w') as f:   # truncates immediately
    f.write(json.dumps(config))
# returns before the data is on disk
cards.answer: `write` returns once data is in the kernel page cache, not on disk; a crash before writeback loses it, and truncating the file first means a crash mid-write leaves it empty. Write to a temporary file in the same directory, `fsync` it, atomically `rename` it over the original, then `fsync` the directory.
cards.explanation: `rename` within one filesystem is atomic, so readers see either the old or the new file, never half of each. Databases, package managers and editors all use this write–fsync–rename dance; skipping any step has caused real data loss.

cards.prompt: What is the page cache, and why does `free` show so little "free" memory on a healthy server?
cards.answer: The kernel caches file data in otherwise unused RAM, so repeated reads come from memory and writes are buffered before reaching disk. This memory is reclaimed instantly when applications need it, so "available" — not "free" — is the number that matters.
cards.explanation: Unused RAM is wasted RAM, so Linux fills it with cache. It is also why the second run of a job is faster, why benchmarks must control for a warm cache, and why databases tune how they share memory with the page cache.

modules.name: Boot, Interrupts & Virtualisation
modules.description: The boot sequence, interrupts and drivers, hypervisor types, capabilities and the security model.

cards.prompt: What happens between pressing the power button and a login prompt on a Linux machine?
cards.answer: Firmware (UEFI) initialises hardware and loads a bootloader (GRUB, systemd-boot) from the EFI partition; the bootloader loads the kernel and an initramfs; the kernel initialises drivers, mounts the real root filesystem with help from the initramfs, and starts PID 1 (systemd), which brings up services in dependency order up to a login target.
cards.explanation: Secure Boot verifies signatures along this chain so tampered bootloaders or kernels refuse to run. `systemd-analyze blame` shows which services slow boot; failures before PID 1 usually point at the initramfs or root filesystem mount.

cards.prompt: What is an interrupt, and how does it differ from polling?
cards.answer: A hardware signal that makes the CPU pause its current work and run the kernel's handler — a key press, a packet arriving, a disk request completing. Polling instead repeatedly checks a device's status. Interrupts avoid wasted cycles when events are rare; polling wins when they are constant.
cards.explanation: At very high rates interrupts themselves become the overhead, so network drivers switch between interrupts and polling (Linux NAPI), and high-performance stacks such as DPDK and io_uring polling mode poll deliberately. Handlers do minimal work immediately and defer the rest.

cards.prompt: Type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors
cards.answer: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware and hosts guest VMs; a type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a normal host OS.

right.title: Type 2 (hosted)
points: Runs on top of a host OS

cards.explanation: Hardware virtualisation extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) and nested page tables made VMs nearly native speed. The lines blur: KVM turns Linux itself into a type 1 hypervisor, and Hyper-V runs underneath Windows when WSL2 is enabled. MicroVMs (Firecracker) boot in milliseconds for serverless isolation.

cards.prompt: What are Linux capabilities and seccomp, and why do containers use them?
cards.answer: Capabilities split root's powers into units (`CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`…) that can be granted or dropped individually. seccomp filters which system calls a process may make at all. Container runtimes drop most capabilities and apply a default seccomp profile.
cards.explanation: Least privilege at the kernel boundary means a compromised process can do far less. `--privileged` re-grants everything and disables these protections, so it should almost never appear in production. `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` is nearly equivalent to full root.
